newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya reformers to stage weekend rally in Mombasa.
newsitem.headline: Kenya reformers to stage weekend rally in Mombasa.

text.p: Kenya protest leaders said on Monday they would hold another "illegal" rally in the coastal resort of Mombasa on Saturday in a campaign for constitutional reform.

Their announcement came as hundreds of heavily-armed police patrolled a section of Nairobi to prevent a third day of rioting. The government blamed hawkers for weekend riots and banned them from the city centre.

The riots started when police broke up a banned opposition rally on Saturday which was called by a coalition of opposition parties, civic societies and church leaders to press for a minimum package of constitutional reform before elections this year.
Nairobi's central business district was quiet on Monday as the country enjoyed a public holiday.

President Daniel arap Moi told a state rally on Sunday there could be no constitutional change before elections but added the Public Order Act regulating public meetings would be replaced by a new bill whose details were not disclosed.

"We will continue to demonstrate to the president that Kenyans want minimal reforms before the general elections," lawyer Gibson Kamau Kuria of the coalition National Convention Assembly (NCA) told a news conference on Monday.
"The next meeting will be in Mombasa this weekend. Others will follow in both Nairobi and the provinces," he added. "We believe we can persuade Moi to effect these reforms."
Human rights group Amnesty International welcomed Moi's statement but said repressive laws like the Public Order Act should be repealed.

"Even with the proposed amendment of this Act the president would retain wide powers to limit the human rights stipulated in the constitution," Pierre Sane, Secretary General of the London-based group said in a statement faxed to Reuters.

"It's about time that Kenya breaks with its colonial legacy by repealing oppressive laws enacted at the time to deprive Kenyans from the fundamental freedoms enshrined in the United Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights," Sane said.
At least 133 people were arrested during weekend rioting and would be charged with "criminal offences", the government said in a statement read on state-run radio and television.
"Hawkers and idlers actively participated in the acts of lawlessness triggered by the illegal meeting organized by the opposition activists," the statement said.
A government order last month that street traders relocate to designated areas outside the centre was largely ignored.

"I think that the (government) statement is hogwash... Hawkers have been in town for a long time and there has been no rioting," Raila Odinga, leader of the National Development Party of Kenya told Reuters.
Odinga and Kuria said the shadowy "Jeshi la Mzee" (Moi's Army) group of youths supposedly recruited by the ruling party to cause trouble was behind much of the looting.

A total of 22 policemen and dozens of civilians were injured during the rioting, 61 shops were looted, two cars were burnt and dozens of others stoned, the government said. One person was stabbed to death, according to newspaper reports.
Opposition leaders were detained at their houses for more than 10 hours to prevent disruption of Moi's speech on Sunday.
The NCA wants six pre-independence laws, including the Public Order Act, scrapped. They also demand greater access to state-run media and an Independent Electoral Commission.

Moi, Kenya's president since 1978, must call elections before the end of the year, pitting his ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU) party against an opposition fractured by ethnic and personal differences.
